title: two Error classes in one failure channel whose durable contract identities collide are rejected, not silently merged into one variant
notes: specification/failures.mdx:209 (Locked): 'Handler selection MUST use compiler-stable nominal identity, not a forgeable user _tag or minifier-sensitive constructor name in compiled artifacts.' Read across the durable boundary, an identity is the key a decoder on the far side selects a handler by, so stability without INJECTIVITY is worthless: two declared Error classes arriving under one identity is precisely a forgeable key, and a decoder handed one of them would run the other's handler. `an-actions-failure-channel-mints-one-identity-per-error-class` pins the benign half of that obligation (two classes, two identities). This case pins the hostile half, and it is the half a compiler can only satisfy by refusing. `$Failed` and `_Failed` are two distinct declarations whose durable CONTRACT identities normalize to one string; both backends must refuse the program rather than mint a colliding pair. WHAT THIS CASE PINS: the code and the authored position, on both backends. Column 10 on line 20 is the `Pick.run(...)` call node. WHAT IT DELIBERATELY DOES NOT PIN, and this is the important half: the diagnostic MESSAGE. Both backends currently emit 'higher-order and dynamic calls are unavailable in durable source lowering', which is FALSE of this program — there is no higher-order call and no dynamic call in it; `Pick.run({ key: input.key })` is an ordinary compiler-bound Action call. The reference reaches that sentence by falling through to the generic tail of `lowerExpression` (poc/src/durable/source-compiler.ts:1213) rather than by a purpose-built collision diagnostic, and the Go fork reproduces the sentence verbatim to hold backend agreement. So the verdict is right and the stated reason is a swallow artifact, in two places. Declaring `messageContains` here would ratify that misdescription as the contract and make the eventual repair — a diagnostic that actually says two error classes collide — a corpus break for a reason no specification sentence states. The wrong-reason defect is recorded as its own finding; this case is written so that fixing it does not require touching this file. WHAT IS NOT A GAP: the same-NAME family (two classes both spelled `Failed`) is not filed as a case. Both backends refuse it, but at different codes — SMITHERS1150 on the fork, SMITHERS4100/4112 on the reference — which is a both-closed divergence in reasoning, not a fail-open, and pinning it would freeze two unrelated rules against each other. VERIFIED LOAD-BEARING, not assumed: mutating the declared line from 20 to 21 turns the case red on BOTH backends with the position diff printed, and the file was restored byte-identically (sha256 5e911ca9892c2f5f272da542da78557d292990f7ffab0c0a54f89ae9ee439d6d before and after). The paired negative control is `two-error-classes-with-distinct-durable-identities-compile`, which holds the other direction: it must keep compiling and RUNNING on both backends, so a collision check that over-fires on any two error classes turns that case red instead of passing silently. Before the Go identity fix this case could not have been written: the fork's `actionFor` set the error schema from a legacy placeholder and never read an Action's declared failure channel at all, so it compiled and ran this program.
